citations.quote: A **filtered chain complex** $(C,d,F)$ in an abelian category is a chain complex with increasing filtrations $F_pC_n\subseteq C_n$ for all $n$, whose pieces form subcomplexes. Explicitly $d_n$ factors as $F_pC_n\to F_pC_{n-1}$ on each piece. These restrictions square to zero since their composites with the monic inclusion into $C_{n-2}$ are $d_{n-1}d_n=0$. The conventions are [[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]] and [[def-subcomplex]]. Thus, in modules, the condition is exactly $d_n(F_pC_n)\subseteq F_pC_{n-1}$; a factorization implies the inclusion, and the inclusion defines the restricted function. No finite-bound hypothesis is implicit.

If the filtration on every $C_n$ is finite, the spectral sequence of the filtered chain complex stabilizes pointwise and naturally abuts to $H_n(C)$ with its image filtration. This homology filtration is finite, exhaustive and separated. No uniform filtration bound in n is required.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link (a finite disjoint union of oriented smoothly embedded circles,
[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]) with $r\ge1$ components,
and let $X_L:=S^3\setminus L$. Then $X_L$ is a connected smooth $3$-manifold
without boundary, and in particular is path-connected, locally path-connected
and semilocally simply connected; moreover $X_L$ has the homotopy type of a
finite CW complex
([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]). Consequently the
covering-space classification
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]) applies to $X_L$.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

Under the hypotheses of [[prop-covering-morphism-subgroup-criterion]], the based connected coverings $(E_1,e_1)$ and $(E_2,e_2)$ are isomorphic over $B$ if and only if

$$(p_1)_*\pi_1(E_1,e_1)=(p_2)_*\pi_1(E_2,e_2).$$

The based isomorphism, when it exists, is unique.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty finite oriented smooth link in the standard oriented three-sphere, and put $X_L=S^3\setminus L$. A small meridian about $K_i$ is the boundary of a normal disk fiber; its orientation is immaterial modulo two. The mod-two meridian character is the homomorphism $\epsilon_L:\pi_1(X_L)\to\mathbb Z/2$ that sends every component meridian to $1$. For each $K_i$, choose an oriented tubular chart, meaning a diffeomorphism from a normal disk bundle onto a neighborhood, written $\varphi_i:(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times D^2\to N_i$ and respecting the core orientation. Let $\lambda_i$ be the parallel longitude given by $\varphi_i((\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times\{z_0\})$ for a fixed $z_0\in\partial D^2$, and set $\eta_i=\epsilon_L([\lambda_i])\in\{0,1\}$. The double branched cover $\Sigma(L)$ is the closed three-manifold obtained by taking the connected two-sheeted cover of $X_L$ classified by $\ker\epsilon_L$ and extending it over each $K_i$ with local normal-disk model $(s,z)\mapsto(s,e^{\mathrm i\eta_i s}z^2)$ in these coordinates. Give its total space the orientation for which the covering map is orientation-preserving away from the branch locus.

derivations.claim: Compose the Hurewicz isomorphism in [F2], the Alexander-duality isomorphism in [F1], and coordinate-sum modulo two on $\mathbb Z^r$. The local intersection description in [F1] sends a meridian of $K_i$ to $\pm e_i$, whose coordinate sum is $1$ modulo two. This defines $\epsilon_L$ and proves it is surjective because $r\ge1$; hence its kernel has index two.

An ambient isotopy from $L$ to $L'$ restricts to an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of their complements and carries each meridian class to a meridian class. It therefore carries $\ker\epsilon_L$ to $\ker\epsilon_{L'}$.

By [F3] and [F4], the index-two kernel determines a connected two-sheeted cover. On the boundary of a punctured tube around $K_i$, its two monodromies are the prescribed meridian value $1$ and a longitude value $\eta_i\in\mathbb F_2$. The local model [F5] has exactly those two monodromies; classification of covers of the punctured tube identifies it with the restricted cover. The displayed model therefore extends the cover across every branch component. If a tubular framing is changed by $k$ meridional twists, the parallel longitude changes by $k\mu_i$, so its character changes by $k$ modulo two; the corresponding rotation of the normal coordinate changes the phase in the local model by the same parity. Thus these are coordinate descriptions of one extension, not different covers.

The based covering uniqueness in [F4] identifies the two complement covers over this diffeomorphism. The identification extends over each branch tube because it preserves the two boundary monodromies in step 2.1; the local order-two models then give an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the closed branched covers. Thus $\Sigma(L')\cong\Sigma(L)$ as oriented manifolds.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every nonempty compact
connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold is homeomorphic to exactly one
of the following types: the sphere $S^2$, a connected sum of $g\geq1$ tori,
or a connected sum of $k\geq1$ real projective planes. The connected sums here

gluings ([[def-connected-sum-of-compact-surfaces]]). The integer is unique
within its type. Equivalently, two such surfaces are homeomorphic if and only
if they have the same integral orientability and Euler characteristic.

The canonical one-face words are respectively the sphere digon $aa^{-1}$
(whose *reduced notation* is empty), the $g$-fold commutator word
$\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1} b_i^{-1}$, and the $k$-fold square word

Its extension across the two branch points is a compact connected orientable surface with boundary by [F1]–[F2]. Triangulate the disk with both branch points as vertices. A triangulated $m$-gon with a fan from one vertex has $V=m$, $E=2m-3$, and $F=m-2$, hence Euler characteristic $1$; inserting a branch point by subdividing a face preserves the alternating cell count. Lifting cells gives two lifts of every open cell away from the two branch vertices and one lift of each branch vertex, so the extended cover has Euler characteristic $2\cdot1-2=0$. The boundary loop encloses both branch points, so its monodromy is $1+1=0$ in $\mathbb Z/2$; a two-sheeted cover of the boundary circle with trivial monodromy has two boundary circles. Cap those two boundary circles with disks. The resulting closed connected orientable surface has Euler characteristic $0+1+1=2$, so [F3] identifies it with $S^2$. The original surface is the complement of the interiors of those two disjoint cap disks; [F4] identifies the region between their boundary circles as an annulus.
Since the arcs are the product $A=\{a_1,a_2\}\times[0,1]$, the branched cover of $(B,A)$ is the product of the annulus in step 1.1 with $[0,1]$. An annulus times an interval is a solid torus.

Let $F$ be an oriented smooth surface and let $c:S^1\hookrightarrow F$ be a smooth embedded circle. Choose an annular coordinate map $\phi:S^1\times[-1,1]\to A\subset F$ whose product orientation agrees with the orientation of $F$ and whose core $\phi(S^1\times\{0\})$ is $c(S^1)$. Choose a smooth function $\rho:[-1,1]\to[0,1]$ that is $0$ near $-1$ and $1$ near $1$. The positive **Dehn twist about $c$ in the chosen annular coordinates** is the diffeomorphism that is the identity outside $A$ and on $A$ is
$$
\phi(e^{i\theta},t)\longmapsto\phi(e^{i(\theta+2\pi\rho(t))},t).
$$
The negative Dehn twist is its inverse. The annular coordinates and cutoff are part of the data whenever a representative diffeomorphism is used; its mapping class is its class under smooth isotopy through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $F$.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, let $\alpha:I\to B$ be a path, and let $e_0\in E$ satisfy $p(e_0)=\alpha(0)$. There is a unique path $\widetilde\alpha:I\to E$ with $\widetilde\alpha(0)=e_0$ and $p\circ\widetilde\alpha=\alpha$.
Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, $H:Y\times I\to B$ a homotopy, and $\widetilde H_0:Y\to E$ a lift of $H(-,0)$. There is a unique lift $\widetilde H:Y\times I\to E$ of $H$ extending $\widetilde H_0$.

derivations.claim: **An explicit oriented branched annulus.** Fix $c>0$ and put $A=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times[-c,c]$, oriented by $d\theta\wedge dt$. Its complex coordinate is $z=e^{-t+i\theta}$, whose complex orientation is this same orientation. The holomorphic map $$q(z)=z+z^{-1}=(2\cosh t\cos\theta,-2\sinh t\sin\theta)$$ identifies $A$ with a two-fold branched cover of the closed ellipse $D_c$ having semiaxes $2\cosh c,2\sinh c$. Its deck map is $\jmath(\theta,t)=(-\theta,-t)$, and its two fixed points map to $2,-2$. To verify its image and degree, every point outside the real segment $[-2,2]$ lies on a unique confocal ellipse: the expression $x^2/(4\cosh^2t)+y^2/(4\sinh^2t)$ decreases strictly from a value greater than one to at most one as $t$ increases from zero to $c$. Its two preimages have coordinates $(\theta,t)$ and $(-\theta,-t)$. Points inside that segment have the two preimages on $t=0$, except its endpoints. The derivative $1-z^{-2}$ vanishes precisely at $z=\pm1$; locally $q(z)-2=(z-1)^2/z$ and $q(z)+2=(z+1)^2/z$, so each is a simple square branch in smooth complex coordinates. Both boundary components map diffeomorphically to the ellipse boundary.

**A commuting twist.** Choose a smooth nondecreasing $\rho:[-c,c]\to[0,1]$, zero near $-c$, one near $c$, equal to $1/2$ on $[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$ for some $0<\epsilon<c$, and satisfying $\rho(-t)=1-\rho(t)$. For example choose its upper half from a smooth step and reflect. Set $T(\theta,t)=(\theta+2\pi\rho(t),t)$. The symmetry makes $T\jmath=\jmath T$ modulo $2\pi$, since $2\pi\rho(-t)=2\pi-2\pi\rho(t)$. It therefore descends to a smooth disk map $h$ fixing the ellipse boundary. Near either branch it is $q\mapsto-q$, because $T$ adds $\pi$ in the central strip, so descent is smooth there as well. In particular $h$ interchanges the branch points, and $T$ fixes both annular boundaries pointwise. By [F1], $T$ is exactly a positive annular twist. It remains to prove the handedness of its quotient, rather than infer it merely from the interchange.

**An orientation-preserving disk coordinate.** On the quotient of $t\ge\epsilon$ write $\varphi=-\theta$. Then $q=(2\cosh t\cos\varphi,2\sinh t\sin\varphi)$. Choose $r_0\in(0,1)$ and a smooth increasing $t(r)$ from $\epsilon$ to $c$ on $[r_0,1]$. Define $a(r)=2\cosh t(r)$ and $b(r)=2\sinh t(r)$ there. Extend $a,b$ to $[0,1]$ so $a(0)=b(0)=0$, both derivatives are strictly positive, and both are linear near zero. Here is a finite smooth construction: retain their positive derivative germs near $r_0$, on an interval so short that each derivative integral is less than half its prescribed value at $r_0$. Extend each derivative positively and constantly near zero, initially with total integral smaller than that value. Add a nonnegative bump in the intervening interval, with its unique scalar chosen to make the integral equal to that value. Integrating now matches every derivative and the value at $r_0$. Thus $$F(r,\varphi)=(a(r)\cos\varphi,b(r)\sin\varphi)$$ is a smooth odd diffeomorphism from the round disk to $D_c$. Smoothness and invertibility at zero follow from its positive diagonal linear formula there. Away from zero its Jacobian is $a'b\cos^2\varphi+ab'\sin^2\varphi>0$. The ellipses are strictly nested, so the equation $x^2/a(r)^2+y^2/b(r)^2=1$ proves global injectivity and surjectivity. Thus these are actual orientation-preserving disk coordinates, with both branch points inside $r<r_0$.

**The quotient is the positive half-twist, with its sign.** On the central ellipse $h(w)=-w$, and oddness of $F$ makes this the polar rotation $\varphi\mapsto\varphi+\pi$. On an outer confocal ellipse, $T$ changes $\varphi$ by $-2\pi\rho(t)$, which modulo $2\pi$ is the angle $2\pi(1-\rho(t))$. Consequently in the single disk coordinate of step 2.2, $$F^{-1}hF(r,\varphi)=(r,\varphi+\pi\chi(r)),$$ where $\chi=1$ for $r\le r_0$ and $\chi(r)=2(1-\rho(t(r)))$ outside. This is smooth, one near the branch points, and zero near the boundary. The isotopy replacing the angle by $s\pi\chi(r)$ moves the two points counterclockwise through $+\pi$ in an orientation-preserving coordinate. Thus it is the standard positive half-twist, not its inverse. This explicitly fixes the relative sign with the positive annular twist in [F1].

**Transport to the given cover and lift uniqueness.** Apply the preceding model in an oriented coordinate disk supporting the given half-twist. Its branched cover is identified with the model without a covering-classification choice axiom: slit the disk along two disjoint intervals joining the branch points to its outer boundary. Over the resulting simply connected slit disk the two sheets are obtained by unique path lifting from one specified sheet point; endpoints are independent of path by homotopy lifting in [F2]. Crosswise gluing of the two slit banks is forced by the nontrivial monodromy of a small branch meridian, as the local square map shows. This is exactly the gluing of the model. The identifications are smooth locally. At the slit endpoints use the compatible base and source square charts of the chosen representative; the lifted identifications are then linear in the local square-root coordinates and fill smoothly. Outside the support disk its two exterior sheet collars are retained. The two possible lifts differ by $\jmath$; this deck map interchanges the two boundary components, while $T$ fixes them. Thus precisely one lift fixes the annular boundary pointwise, and it is the transported $T$. Only one finite initial sheet choice was made.

**Representatives and orientations.** Any change of smooth half-twist cutoff is an isotopy through the displayed angle functions, constant near the two points and the outer boundary. Lift it by [F2], using the boundary-fixed sheet. On the complement of the branch points, ordinary smooth local covering coordinates make the lift smooth. Near the branch points the isotopy is the fixed half-turn representative; it therefore extends in the square coordinates and is stationary there. More generally the same argument transports a supplied supported coordinate isotopy defining another standard representative of this half-twist class, chosen standard in the branch charts throughout. It gives a smooth relative-boundary isotopy of lifts. If the annular orientation is reversed, change $\theta$ to $-\theta$ while retaining $t$; the actual formula for $T$ becomes $(\theta,t)\mapsto(\theta-2\pi\rho(t),t)$. It is the inverse twist in the positively oriented annular convention. Conversely reversing the half-twist motion reverses this angle. These calculations prove the full orientation and standard-representative assertions and also explain why the other, boundary-swapping lift was excluded. The assertion concerns this smooth mapping-class lift; it does not assert that an arbitrary unnormalized smooth base germ has a smooth square-root lift.

Assume countable choice. On the flat complex torus $T=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$ let $\alpha$ be the image of the real line, and for $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ let $\beta_\varepsilon$ be the image of the line of direction $1+3\varepsilon i$. Then
$$\alpha\cap\beta_\varepsilon=\{(0,0),(1/3,0),(2/3,0)\}\pmod{\mathbb Z^2}.$$
For any basepoint off the circles, every integral periodic domain with zero coefficient at that basepoint is zero; here a periodic domain is a region two-chain whose boundary is an integral sum of the two full circles. Thus this diagram satisfies even the global mixed-sign admissibility condition.

By a relative disk from $x$ to $y$ mean a continuous map from a closed disk with two marked boundary points to $T$, taking the two boundary arcs into $\alpha,\beta_\varepsilon$ and their endpoints to $x,y$. If $x\ne y$, no such disk exists. If $x=y$, every such disk is homotopic to the constant disk at $x$, through maps with the same boundary conditions and fixed endpoints.

Every actual smooth finite-energy strip for the flat equation $u_s+i u_t=0$, with its two boundary edges on these circles and uniform intersection-generator ends, is constant. The actual linearization at any constant strip is a bounded real Hilbert isomorphism $H^1_{\alpha,\beta_\varepsilon}\to L^2$, and therefore has real index zero. In particular every moduli space of index-one finite-energy strips is empty, for any basepoint away from the curves. The corresponding diagram-level mod-two count operator is zero on its three generators, so its chain homology has dimension three. This is an actual calculation for the specified diagram; it does not supply closed-manifold move invariance or identify that homology for every diagram.

Let $L_0,\ldots,L_{n-1}$ be finitely many attaching product tori. Choose one interior point $q_R$ of each region cut out by all their attaching curves, and include any prescribed basepoints in this finite protected list. Let $D$ be a closed neighborhood of the repeated-point locus and these incidence divisors, disjoint from all the product tori. Write $\omega$ for the descended product area form off the repeated-point locus.

Let $u$ be a smooth finite-energy polygon on an actual punctured half-plane source with these successive boundary labels and uniform transverse corner limits. Suppose its source-dependent structure $J_z$ equals $\operatorname{Sym}^m(j)$ on one fixed open neighborhood of $D$ and tames $\omega$ elsewhere, with uniform taming and coefficient bounds. citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty finite oriented smooth link in the standard oriented three-sphere, and put $X_L=S^3\setminus L$. A small meridian about $K_i$ is the boundary of a normal disk fiber; its orientation is immaterial modulo two. The mod-two meridian character is the homomorphism $\epsilon_L:\pi_1(X_L)\to\mathbb Z/2$ that sends every component meridian to $1$. For each $K_i$, choose an oriented tubular chart, meaning a diffeomorphism from a normal disk bundle onto a neighborhood, written $\varphi_i:(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times D^2\to N_i$ and respecting the core orientation. Let $\lambda_i$ be the parallel longitude given by $\varphi_i((\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times\{z_0\})$ for a fixed $z_0\in\partial D^2$, and set $\eta_i=\epsilon_L([\lambda_i])\in\{0,1\}$. The double branched cover $\Sigma(L)$ is the closed three-manifold obtained by taking the connected two-sheeted cover of $X_L$ classified by $\ker\epsilon_L$ and extending it over each $K_i$ with local normal-disk model $(s,z)\mapsto(s,e^{\mathrm i\eta_i s}z^2)$ in these coordinates. Give its total space the orientation for which the covering map is orientation-preserving away from the branch locus.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty finite oriented smooth link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$, the homomorphism $\epsilon_L:\pi_1(S^3\setminus L)\to\mathbb Z/2$ sending every component meridian to $1$ is well-defined and surjective. Its connected cover extends over the link with a simple order-two branch model, independently of the tubular charts used to describe that model. If $L'$ is ambient isotopic to $L$, the resulting oriented branched covers $\Sigma(L')$ and $\Sigma(L)$ are orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic.

Let $B=D^2\times[0,1]$ be a three-ball and let $A=\{a_1,a_2\}\times[0,1]$ be the trivial pair of vertical properly embedded arcs, with $a_1\ne a_2$ in the interior of $D^2$. The connected two-fold cover of $B\setminus A$ whose meridians about both arcs have monodromy $1\in\mathbb Z/2$ extends across $A$ as a simple branched cover, and its total space is a solid torus.

Let $\tau$ be the positive half-twist mapping class of a disk interchanging two marked branch points and fixed near the disk boundary. Choose its standard supported half-turn representative in coordinates compatible with the local branched square charts, and take its unique smooth lift to the connected two-fold branched cover which fixes the annular boundary pointwise. Its smooth isotopy class relative to that boundary is the positive Dehn twist about the core when the half-twist orientation agrees with the annular orientation, and is the inverse twist when the orientation is reversed. A positive half-twist here is the usual supported rotation through $+\pi$ in an oriented disk coordinate containing the two points, interpolated to the identity outside that coordinate disk; the assertion is independent of its cutoff representative.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. An oriented lens space is an oriented closed $3$-manifold obtained by gluing two solid tori by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism. For coprime integers $p>0$ and $q$, let $L(p,q)$ denote the oriented union of the exterior of the unknot in the oriented $3$-sphere and a solid torus whose meridian is identified with the slope $p[\mu_U]+q[\lambda_U]$ on the unknot exterior. Thus this library uses the convention $L(p,q)=E_U(p/q)$; no symbol $L(0,q)$ is assigned.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: **The covered disk pages and their binding fillings.** Use the standard disk open book of $S^3$ about the braid axis $U$: its complement of a small axis neighborhood is $D^2\times S^1$, and the closed two-strand braid meets each disk in two points. This description is explicit in $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$: the axis is $\{z_1=0\}$ and the page parameter is $u=\arg z_1/(2\pi)$; the disk page is parametrized by $z_2$, with $z_1$ having the remaining modulus and chosen argument. Cut the page parameter at zero. The two moving points over the resulting interval are a braid isotopy of the twice-marked disk. Its double branched cover is the corresponding annular product by the same square-coordinate and sheet-gluing construction as [F2]. On gluing the ends, the annular monodromy is the boundary-fixed lift of the braid mapping class, hence $T^k$ by [F3]. There is no extra deck map: the page-parameter loop near the axis bounds a small meridian disk in its neighborhood disjoint from the branch link, and has trivial meridian character. Moreover the axis itself links the two-strand braid twice, so its mod-two character is zero as well. Thus the cover of its solid-torus neighborhood consists of two ordinary copies, one for each annular boundary. In each copy the meridian is the loop $u$ at a fixed boundary-page point. Consequently the whole branched cover is exactly the annular mapping torus with both boundary tori filled along these page-parameter meridians. The local branched models retain the smooth structures.

**Untwist the mapping torus, retaining both meridians.** Write $A=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)_\theta\times[-1,1]_t$, with a positive twist $T(\theta,t)=(\theta+2\pi\rho(t),t)$, where $\rho=0$ near $-1$ and $\rho=1$ near $1$. The mapping torus has the equivalence $(\theta,t,1)\sim(\theta+2\pi k\rho(t),t,0)$. The function $$\theta'=\theta+2\pi k\rho(t)u\pmod {2\pi}$$ is well-defined across that equivalence and gives an actual diffeomorphism of the mapping torus with $S^1_{\theta'}\times[-1,1]_t\times S^1_u$. Its inverse on the cut parameter interval is $\theta=\theta'-2\pi k\rho(t)u$, with the same endpoint compatibility. At the lower boundary the filling meridian $u\mapsto(\theta_0,-1,u)$ has class $(0,1)$ in the $(\theta',u)$ basis. At the upper boundary the corresponding meridian has class $(k,1)$. This computes their actual slopes, not only their intersection number.

**The two solid tori.** Split the product at any fixed interior $t$. Fill its lower end along $(0,1)$. This caps the $u$ circle in the annulus $[-1,t]\times S^1_u$ by a disk, so that piece is the solid torus $V_-=S^1_{\theta'}\times D^2$. Its meridian on the common torus is $m=(0,1)$ and its core longitude is $l=(1,0)$. The upper filled piece is also a solid torus: the integral shear $(\theta',u)\mapsto(\theta'-2\pi ku,u)$ extends over its whole product collar, is single-valued because $k$ is an integer, and takes its filling slope $(k,1)$ to $(0,1)$. After that shear it is the same disk-capped product as the lower piece. Before undoing the shear, its meridian on the common torus is precisely $kl+m$. Hence this is a genus-one gluing with that meridian slope.

**Identify the fixed unknot peripheral basis.** Identify $V_-$ with the standard unknot exterior, using the same $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$ decomposition: $E_U=\{|z_1|\ge\varepsilon\}$ for a small standard axis neighborhood $\{|z_1|\le\varepsilon\}$. On its boundary the unknot meridian $\mu_U$ is the $\arg z_1$ circle, which generates the core circle of $E_U$, and the preferred longitude $\lambda_U$ is the $\arg z_2$ circle, which bounds its meridian disk. Thus take $l=\mu_U$, $m=\lambda_U$ by an actual product-coordinate identification. Up to the global orientation choice allowed in the statement, the other solid torus is attached with meridian $k\mu_U+\lambda_U$. For $k=3$ this is exactly [F4]. For $k=-3$, the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(\overline z_1,z_2)$ reverses the orientation of $S^3$, preserves the unknot, and sends $\mu_U$ to $-\mu_U$ and $\lambda_U$ to $\lambda_U$. It carries the slope $-3\mu_U+\lambda_U$ to $3\mu_U+\lambda_U$ and extends over the filled solid torus by the same meridian identification. Hence the other handedness has the same $L(3,1)$ description up to orientation reversal. Reversing the orientation of the branch knot does not change its mod-two meridian character.

In $E_U$ the group is generated by $\mu_U$ and $\lambda_U$ is trivial, by its product $S^1\times D^2$ coordinates. Gluing the second solid torus kills the slope $k\mu_U+\lambda_U$. By [F5] there are no further relations: a primitive complementary boundary longitude identifies the core generator of the attached solid torus with the corresponding word in the exterior generator, so that generator is eliminated from the pushout presentation. The group is therefore $\langle\mu_U\mid\mu_U^k=1\rangle$, cyclic of order $|k|=3$. All new coordinate and slope calculations were finite; the only inherited choice use is the already declared cover and peripheral-convention branch. This proves both assertions for either oriented trefoil without replacing a meridian-slope calculation by the determinant alone.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

**Input:** a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ and a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on its crossing set. A diagram object is supplied as mathematical input; this procedure does not parse a serialized string.

**Output:** the normalized bigraded Khovanov cochain module $C^{i,j}(D)$ and its candidate differential $d:C^{i,j}(D)\to C^{i+1,j}(D)$, constructed by the following finite instructions.

1. Enumerate every state $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$ once. Form the crossingless resolution by using the A-smoothing at $v(c)=0$ and the B-smoothing at $v(c)=1$.
2. For each state, create one tensor factor of the integral Frobenius algebra for each resolution circle and place the resulting tensor product in cohomological degree $|v|-n_-$ and quantum degree $|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$ for its circle labels $a$.
3. For each state and each crossing $c_j$ with $v(c_j)=0$, create the edge to $v+e_j$. Apply multiplication if that smoothing change merges two circles, comultiplication if it splits one circle, the identity on other tensor factors, and the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. Sum the edge maps out of every state to obtain $d$.
4. Return the finite direct sum of the state modules with these degrees and maps. The square-zero property is the separate local lemma named by `justified_by`.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram, order its crossings as $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and form the direct sum of state modules $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ over all functions $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$. Here $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, each crossing is changed from its A-smoothing at $0$ to its B-smoothing at $1$, and the edge map is the multiplication $m$ for a merge or comultiplication $\Delta$ for a split, multiplied by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ on the edge at $c_j$. The link-surgery filtered module associated to $D$ is the direct sum
$$
C_D=\bigoplus_{I\in\{0,1\}^n}\widehat{CF}(\Sigma(D(I));\mathbb F_2),
$$
with the summand for $I$ in increasing filtration degree $n-|I|$. Choose the subordinate Heegaard multi-diagram, compatible perturbation data and top-generator cycles for successive attaching-curve systems. The diagonal component of the candidate differential is the ordinary hat disk differential. For $I<J$ coordinatewise, sum over every ordered path $I=I_0<I_1<\cdots<I_r=J$ changing one coordinate at each step. Its summand counts the zero-dimensional holomorphic $(r+2)$-gon spaces with input at the $I$ vertex, the selected top-generator cycles between each pair of successive attaching systems, and output at the $J$ vertex. The count includes the allowed source conformal parameters and imposes zero basepoint multiplicity. These are the surgery polygon maps; the component is zero if $I\nleq J$. Thus changing several crossings is a sum over paths and polygon counts, not an arbitrary direct edge map. The increasing filtration is $F_pC_D=\bigoplus_{|I|\ge n-p}\widehat{CF}(\Sigma(D(I));\mathbb F_2)$, extended by zero below $0$ and by $C_D$ at and above $n$. Thus a component increasing $|I|$ lowers its filtration degree and preserves every $F_p$. The cube direction and the reduced Khovanov cochain degree remain separate indices. The polygon-count finiteness, square-zero, and total-homology identifications are justified by the surgery lemma, which labels its actual Ozsváth–Szabó construction and top-input/filling calculations as external inputs, separately from the retained local analytic theorem and finite filtration algebra.

The local smoothing labels are those of Ozsváth–Szabó Figure1: in the chart with northwest–southeast over-strand, 0 joins the two left and two right endpoints, and 1 joins the two top and two bottom endpoints. These become A and B on the mirror chart, respectively. This fixes the convention for the consumers without a diagram-invariance assertion. For $I\in\{0,1,\infty\}^n$ let $Y(I)$ be the simultaneous filling specified by $I$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

citations.quote: A **filtered chain complex** $(C,d,F)$ in an abelian category is a chain complex with increasing filtrations $F_pC_n\subseteq C_n$ for all $n$, whose pieces form subcomplexes. Explicitly $d_n$ factors as $F_pC_n\to F_pC_{n-1}$ on each piece. These restrictions square to zero since their composites with the monic inclusion into $C_{n-2}$ are $d_{n-1}d_n=0$. The conventions are [[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]] and [[def-subcomplex]]. Thus, in modules, the condition is exactly $d_n(F_pC_n)\subseteq F_pC_{n-1}$; a factorization implies the inclusion, and the inclusion defines the restricted function. No finite-bound hypothesis is implicit.

A **homological spectral sequence** in an abelian category ([[def-abelian-category]]), starting at a specified integer $r_0\ge0$, consists of objects $E^r_{p,q}$, maps
$$d^r_{p,q}:E^r_{p,q}\to E^r_{p-r,q+r-1},\qquad d^rd^r=0,$$
for r≥r₀ and p,q∈ℤ, and specified isomorphisms
$$\alpha_r:\frac{\ker(d^r_{p,q})}{\operatorname{im}(d^r_{p+r,q-r+1})}\xrightarrow{\sim}E^{r+1}_{p,q}.$$
The quotient has the meaning of [[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]; no direct sum of the whole family is assumed. The isomorphisms are data. **First quadrant** means the initial page vanishes unless p,q≥0; **third quadrant** means it vanishes unless p,q≤0. **Bounded** means that for each integer n only finitely many initial-page terms with p+q=n are nonzero. These support conditions persist because later terms are subquotients of earlier ones.

For the pages of a filtered complex there is a specified natural isomorphism
$$\alpha_r:H(E^r,d^r)_{p,q}\xrightarrow{\sim}E^{r+1}_{p,q}\qquad(r\ge0).$$
The homology at $(p,q)$ uses the incoming map from $(p+r,q-r+1)$ and outgoing map to $(p-r,q+r-1)$.

If the filtration on every $C_n$ is finite, the spectral sequence of the filtered chain complex stabilizes pointwise and naturally abuts to $H_n(C)$ with its image filtration. This homology filtration is finite, exhaustive and separated. No uniform filtration bound in n is required.

Define the reduced complex by $\widetilde C(D,p)=C(D;\mathbb F_2)/\operatorname{im}X_p$, with the surviving based-circle label $1$ assigned reduced quantum degree $0$ by the shift $\widetilde j=j-1$. Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. $$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$

$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
